notes.title: The ICU lead, answered from the runtime
notes.goal: The locale/ICU stack was the sharpest difference between the run that freezes and the one that works. This build writes down the runtime's own record of which ICU classes actually initialised, at the freeze and at the close, so that difference is measured rather than guessed.
details: Still open: Robot Girlfriend freezes at 8 frames when it is the FIRST app in a fresh launch. Workaround unchanged -- open Lewdest House first, close it, then Robot Girlfriend, and it runs to 700+ frames.

Answered, from the source: the locale parent-chain walk the freezing run's main thread is 24 frames deep in CANNOT fail to terminate. Every branch either drops a component or returns a language-only id, the one native-free table it consults is generated Java, and the id parser advances its index on every character -- so no answer a native could give it makes the chain loop.

Answered, from the log: that walk is not where the app is stuck. The main thread MOVED between the two samples (a HashMap.put inside the bundle cache, then Object.wait in the idle looper), so this is a message it is passing through, and after it the looper had nothing left to do.

Measured, one pair of runs only: the run that freezes has ICU running; the single run that got through had ICUBinary's and LocaleData's class initialisers throw a NullPointerException raised by a native, and ran with ICU dead. That inversion is a correlation, not a proven cause -- the cause is still unnamed.

New: the freeze report and the session close print the initialisation state of every loaded ICU/locale class (never run / running / ran / threw) plus the four that decide whether the app's Java locale work runs at all.
New: the freeze report says how much of the app main thread's Java chain is ICU/locale/text code at the instant it is sampled, next to the spin-vs-wait sample.
Nothing here changes how the app runs: it reads the runtime's bookkeeping and never loads or initialises a class.

notes.title: Following the signal that never arrives
notes.goal: This build writes down everything Husk hands the app -- lifecycle, window, surface and looper -- so the next log of the freeze says which of those never arrived, instead of only that the app is waiting.
details: Still open: Robot Girlfriend freezes at 8 frames when it is the FIRST app in a fresh launch. Workaround unchanged -- open Lewdest House first, close it, then Robot Girlfriend, and it runs to 700+ frames.

Settled this round by comparing the two logs line by line: in the working after-swap run the app's own first frame reaches the screen; in the freezing fresh run the app creates its drawing surface and then never once draws into it. Everything before that is identical, so what is missing is the step that makes the app draw.

Settled: a message is NOT sitting in the looper un-woken. The queue wakes the waiting thread and also re-checks itself every 8 ms; the freezing run's own close proves delivery (the app did run its onPause/onStop/onDestroy, just late).

New: every lifecycle step (onCreate/onStart/onResume/onPause/onStop/onDestroy), every window added or removed, every window-focus delivery, every surface created/changed/destroyed (with size and format) is written to the log as a D/HuskDelivery line.

New: every message posted to the app's looper and every one it takes off is written down too, with the one thing a bare line cannot say -- whether the post woke a thread that was waiting, or whether nothing was waiting and the queue's own 8 ms poll had to pick it up. A post with no matching 'dispatch' is a message the app never took.

New: the freeze report and the close summary now name what was feeding the screen (the app's own renderer, the view system, or the app's own drawing surface) and say plainly whether the app ever drew a frame of its own.
New: the same, for the NDK side -- who prepared a thread's event loop, who woke it, and whether the callback was ever run.
Working in this build: the note you are reading now, everything from the previous build, and the new delivery log. Nothing here changes how the app runs: it records.

notes.title: Naming the Java loop
notes.goal: The freeze report can now name the app's own Java method it is sitting in, and say whether that thread is spinning or waiting.
details: Still open: Robot Girlfriend freezes at 8 frames when it is the FIRST app in a fresh launch. Workaround unchanged -- open Lewdest House first, close it, then Robot Girlfriend, and it runs to 700+ frames.

Best evidence so far: the app is WAITING for something that never arrives, rather than being stuck. The render thread and the engine's main thread are both asleep, and Android's main thread is idle waiting for a message.
New: the freeze report prints the app's own Java call stack -- class and method -- for the render thread, the engine thread and the app's main thread.
New: it samples those threads twice, so a spin can be told apart from a wait.
Fixed: the engine's main thread was being skipped in that report because of how it was looked up.
Working in this build: the note you are reading now, and the fix that stops a closed game showing its own screen after you open another one.

notes.title: The note finally shows, and the freeze gets a stack
notes.goal: Each build's note now actually appears when you open a new one, and the freeze report can name the guest function that is looping.
details: Fixed: a new build's note did NOT appear even though the app knew about it. It was being opened as a pop-up the way iOS silently drops during launch; it is now part of the screen instead.
Settings > This Build still shows the note for the build you are running, any time.
New: the freeze report walks the app's own call stack, so the log names the function that keeps running instead of only showing that a thread is asleep.

notes.title: A closed game stops haunting the screen
notes.goal: A closed app can no longer put its frames on the screen or swallow your taps, and the freeze report now names the threads that used to be invisible.
details: Fixed: after closing one game and opening another, the screen could keep showing the CLOSED game's menu with buttons that did nothing.
The layer can stop a dead app drawing, but it cannot remove a frame iOS has already put on the glass.
The freeze report now lists EVERY thread in the process, including the ones Husk starts itself, with the NAME of the call each thread is blocked in.

notes.title: Seeing the freeze — and yes, updates can be near one-tap
notes.goal: Instruments that can see WHERE the black screen comes from — and the answer to whether Husk can update itself.
details: You asked whether the app can push its own updates: iOS does NOT let an app install an update for itself. There is no such API.

What IS possible: Husk can notice a new build and download it itself, then hand it to an installer, which needs one tap from you. AltStore and SideStore can do the whole thing automatically from the source file the project already ships.

notes.title: The region fix, and a note on every build
notes.goal: The translation layer can adopt the JIT region the app has already secured, so guest libraries can load -- and every build opens with a note saying what it is for.
details: This is the build that got Lewdest House running properly.
In the log, look for 'jni: libjavacore.so JNI_OnLoad' and for the failed to initialize Java/lang/System message to be gone.

notes.title: The engine can use the JIT region
notes.goal: The translation layer now reaches the JIT region directly instead of looking it up by name, so it can finally open its arena.
details: Guest libraries can load for the first time, which is what makes java.lang.System initialise.

notes.title: StikDebug is reachable again
notes.goal: The hand-off to StikDebug no longer depends on a permission check that LiveContainer breaks.
details: Opening stikjit:// is now attempted for real, and iOS own answer is what is reported.
The attach request goes to StikDebug when running inside LiveContainer, where the built-in helper cannot work.

notes.title: The JIT latch is gone
notes.goal: One failed JIT probe at launch no longer uses up this launch only chance at a JIT region.
details: A failed probe is remembered as "nothing answered yet" instead of "give up", so the claim is retried up to 3 times.

notes.title: Downloads tile is back
notes.goal: The 3.0 port is done, and the way to download apps from your computer is visible again.
details: Home shows an always-there Downloads card with a live status line.
The old emulator engine (QEMU) was removed, so the app is about 8% smaller.
